title: Keeping Score
coreMove: Turn a vague hedge word into a specific number so the claim can be checked when the outcome arrives — and so you can no longer reinterpret what you meant after the fact.
sourcePressure: Verbal probability language (likely, possible, serious possibility) allows different audiences to map different odds onto the same sentence, preventing later accountability. Sherman Kent pushed numerical probability into intelligence work precisely to make predictions auditable. Calibration and resolution make judgment visible over time. Brier scoring gives a single measurable number for forecast quality. Foxes — who gather small clues and tolerate contradiction — outperform hedgehogs once there is a scoreboard.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong lesson is 'quantify everything' or 'never use words, always use numbers.' The real move is narrower: numerical language forces the forecaster to confront their own uncertainty rather than hide inside verbal ambiguity — the number changes the forecaster's cognition, not just the audience's interpretation.

sourceAnchors.name: Sherman Kent
sourceAnchors.detail: CIA analyst and chief of the Office of National Estimates who in the 1960s pushed intelligence community to attach numerical probability ranges to verbal probability language (e.g., 'probable' = 75–85%) to reduce interpretive drift across readers and make intelligence assessments auditable over time
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Sherman Kent had watched the same intelligence report mean different things to different readers — he wanted the word 'probable' to stop being a mirror for whatever the reader already believed.

sourceAnchors.name: Glenn W. Brier
sourceAnchors.detail: Meteorologist who in 1950 developed the Brier score — a mathematical method for evaluating probabilistic forecasts by measuring the mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and actual outcomes, with 0 as perfect and 0.5 as chance-level
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Brier's scoring rule did something simple: it let you compare the quality of two weather forecasters in a single number, the way a race splits a field into times rather than impressions.

hook: opening with a statistics lesson — this is about accountability, not math
opening with 'Have you ever said something might happen?' — too vague and coaching-register
counterintuition: 'Being precise sounds overconfident, but it actually makes you more honest' — true but too neat; miss the deeper point that the number changes your own thinking first
tryThisNow: any prompt that says 'estimate the probability of three future events' without explaining how to check them — turns the lesson into a party trick
'Look up a weather forecast and notice how it uses percentages' — too passive, skips the self-accountability mechanism
examples: examples where the only point is 'use a percentage instead of a word' — the required beat must show the forecaster being forced to confront their own uncertainty, not just communicate better
any example domain shared with ch01 or ch02 (no hospital credentialing, no winery, no structural engineering)

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: The chapter is about making the implicit explicit — the examples should feel like they arrive from different angles rather than the same template

exampleSpecs.domain: agricultural weather forecasting co-op where farmers need planting-window predictions
exampleSpecs.audience: a regional crop advisor whose verbal forecasts ('dry spell likely') have been misread differently by different farmers
exampleSpecs.stakes: planting timing for 40 farms; too early means frost risk, too late means yield loss
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the advisor switches from 'dry spell likely next week' to '72% chance of below-average rainfall through day 8' — a farmer who would have heard 'likely' as 90% hears the 72% and decides to hedge with half her fields; the number made the disagreement visible instead of hiding it
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a room of farmers around a table with soil moisture reports spread on it, all leaning in differently on what 'likely' means
mustInclude: the contrast with how the word 'likely' was being heard
mustAvoid: turning this into a weather forecasting tutorial
any domain overlap with ch01 or ch02

exampleSpecs.domain: venture capital firm where a partner asks an analyst to put a probability on whether a portfolio company will hit its Series B milestone
exampleSpecs.audience: an analyst who has been saying 'I think it looks good' for three weeks and is now asked for a number
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: when forced to say 65%, the analyst realizes she has been shading her verbal confidence upward to avoid seeming negative — the number forces her to confront that she has not been saying what she actually thinks
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a one-on-one meeting where the partner slides a blank probability column across a deal memo
mustInclude: the analyst's realization that her verbal hedging had been skewing high
the gap between her verbal tone and the number
mustAvoid: turning it into a pitch meeting scene

exampleSpecs.domain: oncology team giving a prognosis to a family
exampleSpecs.audience: an oncologist who has been using 'guarded prognosis' and 'challenging case' with a family who is taking those words as near-certain bad news
exampleSpecs.stakes: the family's treatment decisions, which hinge on whether they understand 5-year survival as 20%, 40%, or lower
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the oncologist switches to a number — '38% five-year survival at comparable stage and age' — and the family's response shifts; they had been hearing 'guarded' as single digits, and the 38% opens a different conversation about treatment intensity
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a family consultation room, the family's posture already closed around what they think they heard
mustInclude: the family's misread of the verbal hedge
the different conversation the number enables
mustAvoid: making this a medical communication guide
any implication the doctor was wrong before

exampleSpecs.domain: software project delivery where an engineering lead is asked for a ship probability before a stakeholder review
exampleSpecs.audience: a lead engineer who has been saying 'we're on track' at every standup for three weeks
exampleSpecs.stakes: a quarterly board presentation where the product announcement has already been scripted
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: when the product VP asks for an actual percentage, the lead says 55% — a number that contradicts the 'on track' signal and forces a conversation that the verbal hedges had been suppressing for three weeks
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a pre-meeting Slack exchange where the lead has typed 'looking good' for the fourth standup in a row
mustInclude: the three weeks of verbal reassurance that contradicted it
the conversation the number finally opens

exampleSpecs.domain: legislative policy analyst at a think tank asked to estimate the probability of a state bill passing
exampleSpecs.audience: a senior analyst whose written brief uses 'strong likelihood' throughout
exampleSpecs.stakes: a nonprofit that is deciding whether to build a pilot program contingent on the bill passing
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the analyst is asked to put a percentage on 'strong likelihood' for a grant committee — she writes 70%, then reads her brief again and realizes three of her paragraphs imply 90%+ confidence while one caveat implies closer to 50%; the number exposes an inconsistency she had not noticed in her own writing
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a grant committee packet with the brief printed and 'what does strong likelihood mean here?' written in the margin in pencil
mustInclude: the inconsistency within her own brief that the number reveals
the grant committee's decision hinging on it
mustAvoid: political commentary on the specific bill topic
any domain overlap with other chapters

exampleSpecs.domain: competitive rowing coach tracking athlete split-time improvement predictions before a major regatta
exampleSpecs.audience: a coach who has been describing expected improvements to athletes with phrases like 'you should be stronger by the time we get there'
exampleSpecs.stakes: athlete training intensity decisions for the final six weeks before the regatta
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the coach switches to recording specific predicted split-time improvements for each athlete — the process of writing '1.4 seconds per 500m gain' forces him to notice that two athletes he has been privately confident about have insufficient training data to justify better than a 50% confidence estimate
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a training log with a column for predicted split improvement left blank for ten weeks
mustInclude: the switch from verbal to numerical prediction
the discovery of his own overclaiming on two athletes
the six-week decision the numbers now drive
mustAvoid: turning this into a sports performance coaching scene
any overlap with marathon coaching in ch01

skillTargets: translate a verbal hedge into a numerical probability in a new context
identify when verbal probability language is being used to avoid accountability
apply the calibration concept — whether stated confidence matches outcomes over time
distinguish resolution from calibration and explain why both matter
analyze whether a numerical forecast exposes internal inconsistency in a reasoning chain

tryThisNowSpec: Find one claim you made in the last 48 hours using a hedge word — likely, probably, good chance, I think. Write down the specific percentage you actually believe. Then ask: could someone reading that percentage check it when the outcome arrives? If you would reinterpret the percentage after the fact, the number is not specific enough yet — narrow it by 10 points.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that explains the psychological mechanism — why writing a number changes the forecaster's own cognition before it changes the audience's — as a direct analytical aside rather than a scene
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
